raw_response:
I am 40 years old and have farmed these lands in Quzhou for 20 years. My household has three people, and with 600 mu I cannot do everything by hand, so I rely on machines for wheat and maize and hire pickers for cotton and stevia. The wheat went into the ground last October — 400 mu of improved varieties such as Luyuan or Jimai. Now in early spring I will irrigate it three times from my well: the reviving water now, then at jointing, and once more at grain filling. I apply about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus 6 kg of phosphorus and 5 kg of potash, because the soil is getting tired after so many years. Two sprays are enough for wheat — one for weeds and one for aphids or rust if they appear. I rotary tilled before sowing last autumn.

Come June, as soon as the wheat is off, I plant 400 mu of hybrid maize — Denghai 605 or similar. I do not till between wheat and maize; there is no time, and the straw helps keep moisture. Two irrigations are usually enough if the summer rains cooperate, and two pesticide trips: herbicide at sowing and insecticide later if the corn borer appears.

Cotton takes 120 mu. It is hard work, but I have grown it for years and the gin buys local. I rotary till in April, lay plastic mulch, and plant an improved variety. I irrigate three times and spray pesticides about ten times through the season — bollworms, aphids, and spider mites never rest. Cotton needs more potash for the bolls, so I use 8 kg per mu.

The remaining 80 mu is stevia. I started this three years ago because a company signs contracts at the village office and sends a truck each autumn. I transplant in April, irrigate five times — stevia loves water — and spray pesticides four times. It needs less fertilizer than cotton. Dried leaves yield about 275 kg per mu, and the price is better than grain.

That is my plan. I use the well because I cannot wait for rain, but I watch the electricity bill. I do not waste fertilizer anymore — prices are too high.
